title: VeriWorld: A Verifiable Visual SWE-Bench for Spatial Reasoning in 3D Environments
claim: Changing only the interaction protocol, from one action per step to batched actions, sharply raises success under the same task, model and budget.
layout: 2x2 grid of rows (Single vs Batch) with task-setup sidebar; top-to-bottom contrast band
description: A wide figure with a gray task-setup sidebar on the left. It holds a dark system-prompt box for a first-person maze navigation agent, two thumbnails (top-down maze and a brick-wall first-person view), the shared move budget, and a legend of arrows. The main area has two stacked rows. The top row is pink and labeled Single action. The bottom row is green and labeled Batch action. A purple banner between them reads 'Change action span — same channels, same model, same move budget'. Each row has a dark code box showing the observation and action format. It also has a red-outlined (top) or green-outlined (bottom) card for the vision+position (VP) condition, showing a maze map with the path. A blue 'raycast' arrow leads to a second card for the vision+position+raycast (VRP) condition, showing a brick-corridor render and a raycast scan box. Big Pass@1 numbers (0.57, 0.57 vs 0.93, 0.97) with average move counts draw the eye.
caption: Batch control improves performance under both evaluated information channels at an equal move budget. Same task (MazeNavFPS, 30 mazes), same model (Gemini-3.1-Pro), and the same budget of primitive moves for both protocols (125/170/210 moves for 3×3/4×4/5×5 grids): switching the action interface from Single (one move per call) to Batch (3–6 moves per call) lifts Pass@1 from 0.57 to 0.93 under VP (vision + position log) and from 0.57 to 0.97 under VRP (VP + raycast), while Batch uses fewer moves on average.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for spatial tasks such as navigation and manipulation, where they must infer geometry and object relationships from visual input in order to act correctly. Existing benchmarks usually test perception and reasoning in isolation, making it hard to tell whether failures come from visual understanding, downstream reasoning, or the bridge between them. We introduce VeriWorld, a benchmark for spatial reasoning in interactive 3D environments with executable actions and deterministic verification. For task families where all three channels are well-defined, we evaluate matched visual, structured, and combined input conditions on the same instance, environment, and verifier; families without a clean visual/structured/combined split are reported separately. This design supports controlled comparisons of perception, reasoning, and their interaction. Using this setup, we uncover two diagnostic findings. First, models often perform much better when task-relevant information, such as object identity, current state, or target location, is given explicitly than when it must be read from the rendered scene, revealing a recurring visual-to-structure gap. Second, action-space and harness design can change outcomes even under the same task and information condition, showing that interaction protocol is itself a confounding variable. VeriWorld is open-sourced to support reproducible and fine-grained evaluation of spatial reasoning in VLMs.
